event_overview.title: About U.S.-Ireland Relations
event_overview.subject: U.S.-Ireland Relations
event_overview.summary: U.S.-Ireland relations are a bilateral diplomatic relationship shaped by extensive people-to-people links, trade and investment, and cooperation on transatlantic and international issues. Northern Ireland is a recurring political context: the United States supports the 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement, while any constitutional change affecting Northern Ireland is governed by the agreement’s consent-based process rather than by U.S. policy alone.

facts.label: Bilateral framework
facts.value: The United States and Ireland have maintained a Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation since it was signed in Dublin on January 21, 1950, and entered into force on September 14, 1950.

facts.label: Economic relationship
facts.value: The two countries’ relationship includes substantial two-way trade and investment; U.S. policy materials describe Ireland’s European Union membership as an important factor in bilateral discussions of trade and economic policy.

facts.label: Tax treaty
facts.value: A U.S.-Ireland income-tax convention was signed on July 28, 1997; instruments of ratification were exchanged on December 17, 1997.

facts.label: Northern Ireland settlement
facts.value: The 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement underpins Northern Ireland’s peace settlement and institutions. It recognizes that a united Ireland can occur only through consent freely and concurrently given North and South, including the consent of a majority in Northern Ireland.

facts.label: U.S. role in the peace process
facts.value: The U.S. government describes its role as supporting the Northern Ireland peace process and devolved institutions through encouragement of implementation of the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement; the British and Irish governments are the agreement’s co-guarantors.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the specified September 12-13, 2026 developments involving U.S. presidential engagement in Ireland, not the full history of U.S.-Ireland diplomacy, trade, or the Northern Ireland peace process.
